…head this ward.
Examiner and Instructor Chen 陳 comments: The style and reasoning are fluent and lucid; it ought to be placed in the front ranks.
Examiner and Instructor Zhang 張 comments: The diction and reasoning are concise and apt; it ought to head the candidates in this Classic.
Mourning garments are instituted because there is kinship, and they follow the connections of relationship; therefore, moral principle is employed to regulate kinship according to its gradations. Thus, in the way of humanity, nothing is greater than affection for kin. For mourning garments merely serve to manifest kinship connections; if one does not employ benevolence and righteousness to regulate them, how could one know the relative weight of kinship ties? That affection for kin is the greatest principle in the way of humanity has good reason indeed!
Of old, the recorder of the rites held that because human beings have kin, they have mourning garments. Where those garments are heavy, they are not arbitrarily heavy; they are made heavy because of the closeness of the kin. Where the garments are light, they are not arbitrarily light; they are made light because of the degree of the kin. In instituting mourning garments on account of having kin, is there any other reason than this? For in kinship there is mutual linkage: for instance, those who are lower in status or younger wear mourning by virtue of their connection to those who are higher in status or elder. And in kinship there is lineal attachment: for instance, those of secondary birth or collateral branches wear mourning by virtue of their connection to the primary heir and the main line.
Since "kinship means connection" in this manner, how could one not employ benevolence and righteousness to regulate kin? Therefore, benevolence centers on grace: one uses the grace and love of benevolence to follow from one's parents step by step upward to the ancestors. In terms of benevolence, parents are weighty while ancestors are lighter; for instance, even the closest kin have their mourning cut off at one year, yet for parents it is three years—is this not because benevolence makes it weighty? Righteousness centers on decision: one uses the decisive distinctions of righteousness to follow from the ancestors in sequence downward to the deceased father's shrine. In terms of righteousness, ancestors are weighty while parents are lighter; for instance, great-great-grandparents and great-grandparents ought by degree to receive only three-month fine-hemp mourning (sima 緦麻), yet they are elevated to untrimmed sackcloth (zishuai 齊衰)—is this not because righteousness makes it weighty?
Now, instituting mourning garments on the basis of kinship connections, and employing benevolence and righteousness to regulate kin—what part of this is not affection for kin? Therefore, the posthumous elevation of royal ancestors as kings and the performance of ancestral sacrifices are all part of the human…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
道也而親親則為之大治道宗法皆人道也而親親
則為之先記禮者於大傳而言此其欲人慎重於親
親也何其至哉抑觀曲禮有曰夫禮者所以定親疎
决嫌疑別同異明是非也然彼則言制服以禮此則
言制服以仁義何耶蓋仁者恩也義主斷也仁有殺
義有等即禮也學者合而觀之其意實互相發也
論
聖人教人有定本
王惟節
===
同考試官訓導郁批非特議論好而舜與孔子教
人定本發明殆盡
考試官教諭陳批論得其旨筆勢不滯誠有學之
士也
考試官教諭張批議論精研筆力蒼古傑作也
論曰聖人之心天地之心也天地之心至公而
已矣聖人體天地之心亦至公而已矣何也天
地之生人欲其無一人而不歸於至化之中然
不能諄諄然而命之也於是篤生聖人以立教
punctuated:
道也，而親親則為之大；治道、宗法，皆人道也，而親親則為之先。記禮者於《大傳》而言此，其欲人慎重於親親也，何其至哉！抑觀《曲禮》有曰：「夫禮者，所以定親疎，决嫌疑，別同異，明是非也。」然彼則言制服以禮，此則言制服以仁義，何耶？蓋仁者恩也，義主斷也；仁有殺，義有等，即禮也。學者合而觀之，其意實互相發也。

論
聖人教人有定本
王惟節
同考試官訓導郁批：非特議論好，而舜與孔子教人定本發明殆盡。
考試官教諭陳批：論得其旨，筆勢不滯，誠有學之士也。
考試官教諭張批：議論精研，筆力蒼古，傑作也。

論曰：聖人之心，天地之心也。天地之心，至公而已矣；聖人體天地之心，亦至公而已矣。何也？天地之生人，欲其無一人而不歸於至化之中，然不能諄諄然而命之也，於是篤生聖人以立教。
translation_en:
… the Way of Man, and affection for kin is the greatest part of it; the Way of Governance and the lineage system are both the Way of Man, and affection for kin takes precedence in them. When the recorder of rites spoke of this in the Great Treatise (Dazhuan), how supreme was his desire that people show grave care in their affection for kin! Moreover, looking at the Summary of the Rules of Propriety (Quli), it says: "Now ritual is that whereby one determines closeness and distance, resolves suspicions and doubts, distinguishes sameness and difference, and clarifies right and wrong." Yet why does that passage speak of regulating mourning garments through ritual, whereas this passage speaks of regulating mourning garments through benevolence and righteousness? This is because benevolence is kindness, while righteousness governs decisive judgment; that benevolence has gradations of diminution and righteousness has degrees of rank is precisely what ritual is. When scholars examine them together, their meanings actually illuminate one another.

Discourse
The Sages Have a Fixed Foundation in Teaching People
Wang Weijie
Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Yu: Not only is the argumentation good, but the fixed foundations by which Shun and Confucius taught people are elucidated almost exhaustively.
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Chen: The discourse grasps the main purport and the momentum of the brush is uninhibited; he is truly a scholar of learning.
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Zhang: The argumentation is finely researched and the brush strength is vigorous and ancient; it is a masterpiece.

The discourse says: The mind of the sage is the mind of Heaven and Earth. The mind of Heaven and Earth is nothing other than supreme impartiality; the sage embodies the mind of Heaven and Earth, which is likewise nothing other than supreme impartiality. Why is this? In giving birth to humanity, Heaven and Earth wish that there be not a single person who does not return within supreme transformation, yet they cannot enjoin them with earnest, repeated words; therefore, they specially give birth to sages to establish teachings. …

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
故聖人之教人亦欲其無一人而不囿於至教
之內自非體天地至公之心能如是乎然其所
以教者亦各因其性分所固有職分所當為而
立為定本耳豈責之以高遠難行之事哉噫天
地之愛夫吾人也亦周矣既賦之以形又畀之
以性形欲其踐也性欲其盡也如此而後人道
盡也然而氣稟不齊形焉不能踐其形性焉不
能盡其性而失其所以為人之道者衆矣天地
於是而生聖人焉聖人之生豈徒然哉聰明睿
===
知厚以質也聖神文武厚以德也作之君師厚
以位也天地之厚於聖人非私也公也非公於
一家公於天下也非公於一世公於萬世也聖
人者出膺天地付託之重任君師教養之寄以
天下之人為吾一體以宇宙內事為吾分內三
綱於我乎維持九法於我乎推布百姓不親曰
吾之責也五品不遜曰吾之責也真能體天地
之心以教人者矣然其所以教者豈有他道哉
亦惟曰有定本而已夫古之教者有六禮七教
punctuated: 故聖人之教人，亦欲其無一人而不囿於至教之內。自非體天地至公之心，能如是乎？然其所以教者，亦各因其性分所固有、職分所當為而立為定本耳，豈責之以高遠難行之事哉？噫！天地之愛夫吾人也亦周矣。既賦之以形，又畀之以性，形欲其踐也，性欲其盡也，如此而後人道盡也。然而氣稟不齊，形焉不能踐其形，性焉不能盡其性，而失其所以為人之道者衆矣。天地於是而生聖人焉。聖人之生，豈徒然哉？聰明睿知，厚以質也；聖神文武，厚以德也；作之君師，厚以位也。天地之厚於聖人，非私也，公也；非公於一家，公於天下也；非公於一世，公於萬世也。聖人者出，膺天地付託之重，任君師教養之寄，以天下之人為吾一體，以宇宙內事為吾分內，三綱於我乎維持，九法於我乎推布，百姓不親，曰吾之責也，五品不遜，曰吾之責也，真能體天地之心以教人者矣。然其所以教者，豈有他道哉？亦惟曰有定本而已。夫古之教者，有六禮、七教、
translation_en:
…Therefore, when the sages instruct people, they likewise wish that not a single person should fail to be encompassed within their supreme teaching. Were it not that they embody the supremely impartial mind of Heaven and Earth, how could they do this? Yet that by which they instruct is simply to establish a fixed foundation for each person according to what is inherent in their allotted nature and what ought to be done in their allotted duty—how could they demand of them things that are lofty, distant, and difficult to practice?

Alas! The love that Heaven and Earth bear toward us humans is indeed comprehensive. Having endowed us with physical form, they also conferred upon us moral nature. As for form, they wish us to fulfill it; as for nature, they wish us to exhaust it. Only when it is thus is the Way of humanity exhausted. Yet endowments of vital force (qi) are not uniform: having form, people are unable to fulfill their form; having nature, they are unable to exhaust their nature; and those who lose the Way of what makes them human are many. Thereupon Heaven and Earth give birth to the sages. Could the birth of the sages be in vain? Perspicacious, clear-sighted, and wise—they are generously endowed with natural qualities; sagely, spiritual, civil, and martial—they are generously endowed with virtue; made rulers and teachers—they are generously endowed with position. That Heaven and Earth are generous toward the sages is not out of partiality, but impartiality; it is not impartial merely toward one family, but impartial toward the whole world; it is not impartial merely for one generation, but impartial for ten thousand generations.

When the sages emerge, they receive the heavy trust committed to them by Heaven and Earth and shoulder the charge of ruling, teaching, and nourishing. They regard the people of the world as one body with themselves, and the affairs within the universe as their own proper duty. By them the Three Bonds are maintained; by them the Nine Categories of the Grand Norm are promulgated. If the hundred surnames are not affectionate, they say, "It is my responsibility"; if the five classes of relationships are not compliant, they say, "It is my responsibility." Truly they are able to embody the mind of Heaven and Earth in instructing people! Yet in that by which they instruct, could there be any other way? It is simply said that there is a fixed foundation, and nothing more. Now, in the instruction of antiquity, there were the Six Rites, the Seven Teachings,…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
八政矣又有三物四教矣而其所謂定本果在
於是乎蓋六禮節此本也七教興此本也八政
防此本也三物達此本也四教明此本也非定
本也然其所謂定本者不外乎五品之人倫與
夫視聽言動之間而已然是本也非由外鑠我
也根原於太極之初具足於性分之內賢非豐
而愚非嗇也古非有而今非無也達非加而窮
非損也奈何伐於斧斤牧於牛羊塞於蓁茅失
其本者多矣故聖人立教因其父子之情薄而
===
或至於相夷也則教之以有親君臣之位失而
或至於相陵也則教之以有敬長幼之序或失
則教之以有序夫婦之道或虧則教之以有別
於朋友也則教之以有信焉聖人之所以教者
非耳提而面命之也振舉於上而下者自化焉
爾目司乎視而或非禮也則教以勿視耳司乎
聽而或非禮也則教以勿聽言焉非禮言之私
也則教以勿言動焉非禮動之私也則教以勿
動聖人之所以教者非家至而日見之也軌範
punctuated: 八政矣，又有三物、四教矣，而其所謂定本，果在於於是乎？蓋六禮節此本也，七教興此本也，八政防此本也，三物達此本也，四教明此本也，非定本也。然其所謂定本者，不外乎五品之人倫，與夫視、聽、言、動之間而已。然是本也，非由外鑠我也，根原於太極之初，具足於性分之內，賢非豐而愚非嗇也，古非有而今非無也，達非加而窮非損也。奈何伐於斧斤，牧於牛羊，塞於蓁茅，失其本者多矣。故聖人立教，因其父子之情薄，而或至於相夷也，則教之以有親；君臣之位失，而或至於相陵也，則教之以有敬；長幼之序或失，則教之以有序；夫婦之道或虧，則教之以有別；於朋友也，則教之以有信焉。聖人之所以教者，非耳提而面命之也，振舉於上而下者自化焉爾。目司乎視，而或非禮也，則教以勿視；耳司乎聽，而或非禮也，則教以勿聽；言焉非禮，言之私也，則教以勿言；動焉非禮，動之私也，則教以勿動。聖人之所以教者，非家至而日見之也，軌範…
translation_en: …and the Eight Regulations, and furthermore there were the Three Things and the Four Teachings; yet did what is called the fixed foundation truly lie in these? For the Six Rites regulate this foundation, the Seven Teachings rouse this foundation, the Eight Regulations safeguard this foundation, the Three Things carry through this foundation, and the Four Teachings illuminate this foundation—they are not themselves the fixed foundation. Rather, what is called the fixed foundation is nothing beyond the human relationships of the five classes and the realm of seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting. Yet this foundation is not fused onto us from outside: it originates in the beginning of the Supreme Ultimate and is fully present within our allotted nature. In the worthy it is not abundant, and in the foolish it is not scant; in antiquity it was not present while in the present it is absent; in success nothing is added to it, and in obscurity nothing is taken from it. How is it, then, that felled by axes and bills, grazed over by cattle and sheep, and choked by thickets and weeds, those who lose their foundation are so many? Therefore the sage establishes instruction: because the affection between father and son grows thin, sometimes to the point of mutual estrangement and harm, he teaches them to have closeness; because the stations of ruler and minister are lost, sometimes to the point of encroaching upon one another, he teaches them to have reverence; when the precedence between elder and younger is lost, he teaches them to have order; when the way of husband and wife is impaired, he teaches them to have distinction; and with friends, he teaches them to have trustworthiness. The means by which the sage instructs is not by holding people by the ear and commanding them face to face; he simply raises and sets these forth above, and those below are transformed of themselves. The eyes govern sight, and when what is seen is contrary to propriety, he teaches not to look; the ears govern hearing, and when what is heard is contrary to propriety, he teaches not to listen; when speech is contrary to propriety, it is the selfishness of speech, and he teaches not to speak; when action is contrary to propriety, it is the selfishness of action, and he teaches not to act. The means by which the sage instructs is not by going to every household and seeing people every day; he sets the standard…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
於此而遠者自效焉爾由是天下之人雖知愚
異稟賢不肖殊科而凡沐浴於吾聖人膏澤之
中者莫不熈熈然敦義以相正也鼓舞於吾聖
人聲敎之內者靡不皥皥然謹禮以相與也百
姓昭明定本明也五典克從定本從也敎化無
窮定本之無窮也人徒見四方風動民協于中
以為聖人敎之使然也而不知天地生聖人篤
倫理以敎天下後世也人徒見天道以明人極
以建以為聖人敎之使然也而不知天地生聖
===
人明天理以敎天下萬世也聖人體天地之心
以敎天下後世則聖人之敎行即天地之敎行
也大哉聖人至公之心乎其與天地之心流通
而無間者乎稽之古人其克當乎此者唯大舜
與吾孔子為然大舜使契為司徒敎以人倫父
子有親君臣有義夫婦有別長幼有序朋友有
信夫子告顏淵曰克己復禮為仁非禮勿視非
禮勿聽非禮勿言非禮勿動朱晦菴有見於此
而曰聖人敎人有定本其言不我欺也其言不
punctuated: 於此，而遠者自效焉爾。由是天下之人，雖知愚異稟，賢不肖殊科，而凡沐浴於吾聖人膏澤之中者，莫不熈熈然敦義以相正也；鼓舞於吾聖人聲敎之內者，靡不皥皥然謹禮以相與也。百姓昭明，定本明也；五典克從，定本從也；敎化無窮，定本之無窮也。人徒見四方風動、民協于中，以為聖人敎之使然也，而不知天地生聖人，篤倫理以敎天下後世也；人徒見天道以明、人極以建，以為聖人敎之使然也，而不知天地生聖人，明天理以敎天下萬世也。聖人體天地之心以敎天下後世，則聖人之敎行，即天地之敎行也。大哉聖人至公之心乎！其與天地之心流通而無間者乎！稽之古人，其克當乎此者，唯大舜與吾孔子為然。大舜使契為司徒，敎以人倫：父子有親，君臣有義，夫婦有別，長幼有序，朋友有信。夫子告顏淵曰：「克己復禮為仁。非禮勿視，非禮勿聽，非禮勿言，非禮勿動。」朱晦菴有見於此，而曰：「聖人敎人有定本。」其言不我欺也，其言不
translation_en: …is set here, and those who are distant naturally emulate it. Because of this, among the people of the world, although the wise and the foolish differ in their innate endowments, and the worthy and the unworthy belong to different categories, all who are bathed in the rich grace of our sages without exception harmoniously esteem righteousness to rectify one another; and all who are inspired within the renown and teachings of our sages without fail contentedly observe ritual propriety in their dealings with one another. That the hundred surnames become illustrious and enlightened is because the fixed foundation is made clear; that the Five Canonically Prescribed Relationships are Harmoniously Observed is because the fixed foundation is followed; that the transforming influence of instruction is inexhaustible is because the fixed foundation is inexhaustible. People merely see the four quarters moved as if by the wind and the populace brought into harmony with the mean, and suppose that the sages' teaching made it so; yet they do not know that Heaven and Earth give birth to the sages to consolidate human moral relations so as to instruct the world and posterity. People merely see the Way of Heaven made bright and the standard of humanity established, and suppose that the sages' teaching made it so; yet they do not know that Heaven and Earth give birth to the sages to clarify the principles of Heaven so as to instruct the world and ten thousand generations. When the sages embody the mind of Heaven and Earth in instructing the world and posterity, then the carrying out of the sages' teaching is none other than the carrying out of the teaching of Heaven and Earth. Great indeed is the supremely impartial mind of the sages! Does it not flow in communion with the mind of Heaven and Earth without the slightest gap? Examining the ancients, those who were truly equal to this were only the Great Shun 大舜 and our Confucius 孔子. The Great Shun appointed Xie 契 as Minister of Education (Situ) to teach the human relationships: that between father and son there should be affection, between ruler and minister righteousness, between husband and wife distinction, between old and young precedence, and between friends faithfulness. The Master told Yan Yuan 顏淵: "To subdue oneself and return to ritual propriety is humaneness. Do not look at what is contrary to ritual propriety; do not listen to what is contrary to ritual propriety; do not speak what is contrary to ritual propriety; do not make any movement that is contrary to ritual propriety." Zhu Huian 朱晦菴 [Zhu Xi 朱熹] perceived this when he said: "In teaching people, the sages have a fixed foundation." His words do not deceive us! His words do not…

translation_en:
…deceive us! Now, the Great Shun was a sage who achieved eminence and occupied a high position; Confucius was a sage who remained in obscurity and occupied a lowly position. Because Shun achieved eminence and occupied a high position, his teachings were put into practice in his own time; because Confucius remained in obscurity and occupied a lowly position, his teachings have been put into practice for ten thousand generations. Shun and Confucius are gone, yet a thousand years later, to embody the mind of Heaven and Earth so as to instruct all people—for this today we are fortunate to have the Sacred Son of Heaven on high.

Memorial

An Imitation of a Song-Dynasty Memorial of Thanks on Appointment as Hanlin Academician, in the Persona of Fan Zhen 范鎮

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
諫登賢俊以盈
朝偃武脩文重詞章於
內苑購遺文而山積幸
聖駕以時臨千載奇逢一朝
盛事此誠建億萬載太平之基業者也臣草茅賤
士樗櫟凡材遽承
紫殿之恩獲
賜玉堂之篆昔知諫院殊無陳善之能今任詞林
忝預登瀛之選舊階之榮已至
===
新命之眷奚堪自揣疎庸深懷戰懼恩如泉注慙
非陸贄之竒才官目氷銜徒冒彭年之美譽顧
涓埃之未答何
雨露之重霑臣敢不罄竭丹衷慎居清要掌
絲綸之出入謹
制誥之精嚴伏願
聖德中天日斯明而月斯朗
皇圖永曆山與峙而川與流共沐
洪休均承
punctuated: 諫，登賢俊以盈朝；偃武脩文，重詞章於內苑。購遺文而山積，幸聖駕以時臨。千載奇逢，一朝盛事，此誠建億萬載太平之基業者也。臣草茅賤士，樗櫟凡材，遽承紫殿之恩，獲賜玉堂之篆。昔知諫院，殊無陳善之能；今任詞林，忝預登瀛之選。舊階之榮已至，新命之眷奚堪！自揣疎庸，深懷戰懼。恩如泉注，慙非陸贄之竒才；官目氷銜，徒冒彭年之美譽。顧涓埃之未答，何雨露之重霑！臣敢不罄竭丹衷，慎居清要，掌絲綸之出入，謹制誥之精嚴。伏願聖德中天，日斯明而月斯朗；皇圖永曆，山與峙而川與流。共沐洪休，均承
translation_en:
… accepts remonstrance, elevating the worthy and talented to fill the court; ceasing military affairs and cultivating civil culture, prizing literary composition in the Inner Gardens. Lost texts have been sought and purchased until they pile up like mountains, and the sacred carriage graces the academy with timely visits. This is a rare encounter of a thousand years, a grand occasion of a single morning—truly the foundation for establishing a hundred million years of great peace!

Your servant is a lowly scholar from the thatched huts, ordinary timber like the ailanthus and scrub oak, yet I have suddenly received the grace of the Purple Hall and been granted the seal of the Jade Hall. Previously, when administering the Bureau of Remonstrance, I utterly lacked the ability to set forth what is good; now, serving in the Forest of Letters, I unworthily share in the selection of those who "ascend Yingzhou." The honor of my former rank was already the utmost; how can I bear the favor of this new appointment! Measuring my own carelessness and mediocrity, I am deeply filled with trembling and fear. Imperial grace pours forth like a spring, yet I am ashamed not to possess the extraordinary talent of Lu Zhi 陸贄; my office is styled an "icy title," yet in vain I usurp the fine reputation of Chen Pengnian 陳彭年. Seeing that I have not yet repaid a single drop or speck of dust, how is it that the rain and dew of imperial favor moisten me once again!

How dare your servant not exhaust his red-hearted loyalty, cautiously occupy this pure and prestigious post, take charge of the issuance of silken imperial words, and carefully maintain the precision and rigor of decrees and mandates! I humbly wish that Your Sacred Virtue may stand at the zenith of heaven, bright as the sun and luminous as the moon; and that the Imperial Plan may endure through eternal ages, towering with the mountains and flowing with the rivers—all bathing together in the vast blessings, and equally receiving…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
大化臣不勝戰慄之至謹上
表稱謝以
聞
策
第一問
林球
同考試官訓導華批文有條理而名實不遺佳策也
考試官教諭陳批隨問而荅整整可觀
考試官教諭張批條荅詳明
===
聖辟明君繼統天位而體元叅化之功先後同一道
天葩睿藻昭布海宇而垂訓立教之道先後同一
心前乎堯舜禹湯文武所以君師天下者此心
此道也後乎我
朝
列聖所以昭示海宇者亦此心此道也請因明問而
畧陳之盖人道之要莫大於五倫故人君立教
之道亦莫先於五倫如堯之以親九族舜之慎
徽五典禹之敷文命湯之脩人紀文王之緝熈
punctuated:
大化。臣不勝戰慄之至，謹上表稱謝以聞。

策

第一問

林球

同考試官訓導華批：文有條理，而名實不遺，佳策也。
考試官教諭陳批：隨問而荅，整整可觀。
考試官教諭張批：條荅詳明。

聖辟明君，繼統天位，而體元叅化之功，先後同一道；天葩睿藻，昭布海宇，而垂訓立教之道，先後同一心。前乎堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武所以君師天下者，此心、此道也；後乎我朝列聖所以昭示海宇者，亦此心、此道也。請因明問而畧陳之。盖人道之要，莫大於五倫，故人君立教之道，亦莫先於五倫。如堯之以親九族，舜之慎徽五典，禹之敷文命，湯之脩人紀，文王之緝熈
translation_en:
… the grand transformative influence. Overcome with trembling awe, your servant respectfully submits this memorial of thanks for the throne's information.

Policy Essays

Question One

Lin Qiu 林球

Comment by Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor Hua 華: "The essay is well-organized and omits neither name nor reality; it is a fine policy essay."

When sage sovereigns and enlightened rulers succeed to the heavenly throne, their achievements in embodying the primal origin and participating in cosmic transformation follow the same Way from generation to generation; when their celestial blossoms of imperial composition are brightly promulgated throughout the realm, their Way of handing down instructions and establishing teachings stems from the same mind from generation to generation. In former times, that whereby Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu acted as rulers and teachers to All under Heaven was this very mind and this very Way; in later times, that whereby the successive sage emperors of our dynasty have clearly instructed the realm within the seas is likewise this very mind and this very Way. Allow me to base myself upon your enlightened question and briefly set this forth. Now, the essentials of the human Way have nothing greater than the Five Cardinal Relationships, and therefore the Way by which a ruler establishes teachings likewise places nothing ahead of the Five Cardinal Relationships. For instance, Yao's bringing harmony to the nine branches of kin, Shun's cautiously beautifying the five constant virtues, Yu's spreading abroad his civilizing mandate, Tang's cultivating the human bonds, King Wen's continuing and brightening…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
敬止武王之重民五教何莫不以是為先務歟
洪惟我
朝誕膺
天命
列聖繼作文教大興
太祖高皇帝御製大誥三編
太宗文皇帝御製孝順事實為善陰隲二書以頒布
中外家傳人誦所以百年之間四海之内聲教
遠曁而人倫無不明矣伏遇
===
宣宗章皇帝光昭聖謨游心典籍又於萬幾之暇采
古今之嘉言善行有關於倫理者萃以成編名
曰五倫書而
英宗睿皇帝克承先烈頒布天下以示勸其立教垂
訓之意盖與堯舜禹湯文武之心
太祖
太宗之意寔同一揆也道豈異乎哉心豈二乎哉生
嘗欽誦所載君道之目五十而始於聖德聖學
以聖德言之其仁如天其智如神就之如日望
punctuated: 敬止，武王之重民五教，何莫不以是為先務歟？洪惟我朝誕膺天命，列聖繼作，文教大興。太祖高皇帝御製《大誥》三編，太宗文皇帝御製《孝順事實》、《為善陰隲》二書，以頒布中外，家傳人誦，所以百年之間，四海之内，聲教遠曁，而人倫無不明矣。伏遇宣宗章皇帝光昭聖謨，游心典籍，又於萬幾之暇，采古今之嘉言善行有關於倫理者，萃以成編，名曰《五倫書》；而英宗睿皇帝克承先烈，頒布天下，以示勸。其立教垂訓之意，盖與堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之心，太祖、太宗之意，寔同一揆也。道豈異乎哉？心豈二乎哉？生嘗欽誦所載，君道之目五十，而始於聖德、聖學。以聖德言之：其仁如天，其智如神，就之如日，望
translation_en:
… reverent resting in the highest good, and King Wu's emphasis on the five teachings for the people—which of them did not take this as their foremost task?

Reflecting on how our Dynasty grandly received the Mandate of Heaven, successive sage emperors have arisen one after another, and cultural education has greatly flourished. The Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu), personally composed the three parts of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao), and the Grand Ancestor, Emperor Wen (Taizong), personally composed the two books, Biographical Accounts of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi) and Secret Merits of Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi), promulgating them inside and outside the court so that every family transmitted them and every person recited them. Thus, within the space of a hundred years, throughout the Four Seas, theirmoral prestige and teachings reached afar, and there were none among the human relationships that were not made clear. Humbly we encountered the Manifest Ancestor, Emperor Zhang (Xuanzong), who gloriously illustrated the sacred plans and let his mind roam in the canonical texts; furthermore, in his leisure from the myriad affairs of state, he gathered fine words and good deeds from antiquity to the present that pertained to moral principles, compiling them into a work entitled the Book of the Five Relationships (Wulun shu). And the Eminent Ancestor, Emperor Rui (Yingzong), was able to carry on the meritorious work of his predecessors, promulgating it throughout the realm to serve as encouragement. Their intention in establishing teachings and handing down instructions truly follows the exact same principle as the minds of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu, and the intentions of the Grand Progenitor and Grand Ancestor. How could the Way be different? How could their minds be two?

I, this student, have reverently recited what is recorded therein: the headings under the Way of the Ruler number fifty, beginning with "Sagely Virtue" and "Sagely Learning." Speaking in terms of Sagely Virtue: he whose benevolence was like Heaven, whose wisdom was like a spirit, whom approaching was like the sun, and whom looking…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之如雲者堯也而克寛克仁克明克忠者非成
湯乎臨下以簡御衆以寛者舜也而不泄邇不
忘遠者非武王乎是雖有性之身之之殊要之
同一聖德之盛也以聖學言之受丹書於尚父
訪洪範於箕子者武王也開文學館而銳情經
術者非唐太宗乎舊學于甘盤惟克邁乃訓者
高宗也而雖在軍旅手不釋卷者非宋太祖乎
是雖有先後小大之殊要之同一聖學之勤也
臣道之目四十有八而始於輔德經國以輔德
===
言之毋怠毋荒四夷來王伯益之告舜者至矣
而周公作無逸之書賦大明之詩以戒成王者
心豈異乎脩德脩刑動天以誠宋璟之戒玄宗
者切矣而呂夷簡陳辨佞之言進節費之疏以
告仁宗者意豈異乎以經國言之決九川弼五
服大禹之功茂矣視召穆公之經營四方告成
于王寔同一轍焉辨方正位體國經野周公之
績偉矣視仲山甫之出納王命為王喉舌皆同
一軌焉包拯擢任舘閣戒犯贓濫而刻石三十
punctuated:
之如雲者，堯也；而克寛、克仁、克明、克忠者，非成湯乎？臨下以簡、御衆以寛者，舜也；而不泄邇、不忘遠者，非武王乎？是雖有性之、身之之殊，要之同一聖德之盛也。以聖學言之：受《丹書》於尚父、訪《洪範》於箕子者，武王也；開文學館而銳情經術者，非唐太宗乎？舊學于甘盤，惟克邁乃訓者，高宗也；而雖在軍旅，手不釋卷者，非宋太祖乎？是雖有先後、小大之殊，要之同一聖學之勤也。
臣道之目四十有八，而始於輔德、經國。以輔德言之：「毋怠毋荒，四夷來王」，伯益之告舜者至矣；而周公作《無逸》之書、賦《大明》之詩以戒成王者，心豈異乎？脩德脩刑，動天以誠，宋璟之戒玄宗者切矣；而呂夷簡陳辨佞之言、進節費之疏以告仁宗者，意豈異乎？以經國言之：決九川、弼五服，大禹之功茂矣，視召穆公之「經營四方，告成于王」，寔同一轍焉；辨方正位，體國經野，周公之績偉矣，視仲山甫之「出納王命，為王喉舌」，皆同一軌焉。
包拯擢任舘閣，戒犯贓濫，而刻石三十
translation_en:
… looked up to him as to the clouds: such was Yao; and he who was able to be magnanimous, humane, discerning, and devoted [?]: was that not Cheng Tang? He who oversaw his subordinates with simplicity and governed the multitude with leniency: such was Shun; and he who did not treat the near with familiarity nor forget the distant: was that not King Wu? Although there was between them the difference of possessing virtue by innate nature versus embodying it through personal effort, in sum they shared the same flourishing of sagely virtue. To speak of sagely learning: he who received the Cinnabar Writing (Danshu) from Father Shang [Taigong Wang] and inquired about the Great Plan (Hongfan) from the Viscount of Ji (Jizi): such was King Wu; and he who opened the Institute for the Advancement of Literature (Wenxue guan) and devoted himself earnestly to classical scholarship: was that not Emperor Taizong of Tang? He who had formerly studied under Gan Pan and was able to advance boldly in his teachings: such was Gaozong [King Wu Ding of Shang]; and he who, even while on military campaign, never let a scroll leave his hand: was that not Emperor Taizu of Song? Although there were differences of earlier and later, lesser and greater among them, in sum they shared the same diligence in sagely learning.

The headings under the Way of the Minister number forty-eight, beginning with "Assisting Virtue" and "Ordering the State." To speak of assisting virtue: "Be neither lazy nor negligent, and the four夷 (border tribes) will come to acknowledge your kingship"—the counsel that Boyi gave to Shun was consummate indeed; and when the Duke of Zhou composed the document Against Luxurious Ease (Wuyi) and recited the ode "Bright and Illustrious" (Daming) to admonish King Cheng, how could his heart have been any different? To cultivate virtue and reform punishments so as to move Heaven through sincerity—the admonition that Song Jing 송경 gave to Emperor Xuanzong of Tang was earnest indeed; and when Lü Yijian 呂夷簡 set forth words on distinguishing flatterers and presented memorials on economizing expenditures to advise Emperor Renzong of Song, how could his intention have been any different? To speak of ordering the state: opening the nine rivers and assisting in the establishment of the five domains—the achievements of Great Yu were abundant indeed; compared with Duke Mu of Shao 召穆公, who "planned and managed the four quarters and reported success to the King," they truly followed the very same track. Determining directions and fixing positions, laying out the capital and dividing the wilds—the accomplishments of the Duke of Zhou were magnificent indeed; compared with Zhong Shanfu 仲山甫, who "issued and received the royal commands, serving as the King's tongue and throat," they all followed the very same path.

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
七字以詔其子李襲譽解職揚州囊無餘蓄而
惟以賜田十頃桑千株以遺其後其所遺雖不
同而教子之心則同也父道不亦善乎伯竒見
逐於其母則采檸以食援琴以歌而不敢有怨
大舜不得於其親則往畊于田號泣于天而終
身怨慕其情雖不一而慕親之心則一也子道
不亦盡乎寧忤帝旨不以貴戚易陋妻尉遲敬
德於夫道善矣彼貞姬却白璧黃金之聘辭吳
王夫人之位而守節不渝者婦道何愧焉寧違
===
父命不以寵祿傷天倫叔齊於弟道盡矣彼餘
祭夷昧知季札之賢效泰伯之讓而秉德不回
者兄道何厚焉至若朋友之倫如雷義之於陳
重則相許以膠漆申屠蟠之於王子居則相托
以死生柳宗元之於劉禹錫鮑叔牙之於管夷
吾又皆友道之善而不以利害得失易其心者
也愚生游心校庠欽服
聖訓盖已有日而於五倫之教固將書諸紳而措諸
行矣徒誦說云乎哉徒誦說云乎哉謹對
punctuated: 七字以詔其子；李襲譽解職揚州，囊無餘蓄，而惟以賜田十頃、桑千株以遺其後。其所遺雖不同，而教子之心則同也，父道不亦善乎？伯竒見逐於其母，則采檸以食，援琴以歌，而不敢有怨；大舜不得於其親，則往畊于田，號泣于天，而終身怨慕。其情雖不一，而慕親之心則一也，子道不亦盡乎？寧忤帝旨，不以貴戚易陋妻，尉遲敬德於夫道善矣；彼貞姬却白璧黃金之聘，辭吳王夫人之位，而守節不渝者，婦道何愧焉？寧違父命，不以寵祿傷天倫，叔齊於弟道盡矣；彼餘祭、夷昧知季札之賢，效泰伯之讓，而秉德不回者，兄道何厚焉？至若朋友之倫，如雷義之於陳重，則相許以膠漆；申屠蟠之於王子居，則相托以死生；柳宗元之於劉禹錫，鮑叔牙之於管夷吾，又皆友道之善，而不以利害得失易其心者也。愚生游心校庠，欽服聖訓，盖已有日，而於五倫之教，固將書諸紳而措諸行矣，徒誦說云乎哉？徒誦說云乎哉？謹對。
translation_en:
…seven characters to instruct his sons; Li Xiyu 李襲譽, upon leaving his post in Yangzhou, had no surplus savings in his purse, and left his descendants only the ten qing of granted fields and one thousand mulberry trees. Although what they left behind was not the same, their hearts in instructing their sons were the same—was not the way of the father thus well fulfilled? When Boqi 伯奇 was driven out by his mother, he gathered pear blossoms [?] to eat and took up his zither to sing, not daring to harbor resentment; when the Great Shun 大舜 could not win the favor of his parents, he went to plow in the fields, crying out and weeping to Heaven in lifelong plaintive longing. Although their circumstances were not identical, their hearts in longing for their parents were one—was not the way of the son thus carried to the utmost? Preferring to defy the Emperor's decree rather than replace his humble wife with an imperial relative, Yuchi Jingde 尉遲敬德 was admirable in the way of the husband; and as for Zhenji 貞姬, who rejected betrothal gifts of white jade disks and yellow gold, declined the position of consort to the King of Wu, and maintained her chastity without wavering—what shame had she in the way of the wife? Preferring to disobey his father's command rather than harm heavenly human relationships for the sake of favored emolument, Shuqi 叔齊 carried the way of the younger brother to the utmost; and as for Yuzhai 餘祭 and Yimei 夷昧, who recognized the worthiness of Jizha 季札, emulated the yielding of Taibo 泰伯, and held fast to virtue without turning back—how generous were they in the way of the elder brother! As for the relationship of friends: Lei Yi 雷義 and Chen Zhong 陳重 pledged themselves to each other like glue and lacquer; Shentu Pan 申屠蟠 and Wang Ziju 王子居 entrusted each other with life and death; and Liu Zongyuan 柳宗元 with Liu Yuxi 劉禹錫, and Bao Shuya 鮑叔牙 with Guan Yiwu 管夷吾, all exemplified excellence in the way of friends, never changing their hearts on account of advantage or harm, gain or loss.

Your foolish student has immersed his mind in the state schools and reverently submitted to the Sacred Instructions for many days now; regarding the teachings of the Five Relationships, I shall certainly inscribe them upon my sash and put them into practice. Could it be a matter of mere recitation and talk? Could it be a matter of mere recitation and talk? Your servant respectfully replies.

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
第二問
梁建中
同考試官訓導周批隨問隨荅畧無疑碍非老於性
理者不能歆羡歆羡
同考試官訓導華批援據經傳條荅詳明盖嘗潜
心於理學者
考試官教諭陳批據理條荅畧無所遺
考試官教諭張批敷對無遺必博學之士也
文以載道而六經四書則萬世之至文也學以
===
明道而六經四書則萬世之正學也學者因文
以窮理窮理以明道則聖賢所載之微辭奥義
一以貫之而無疑矣請承明問而畧評之夫六
經四書之行于世猶日月星辰之麗乎天照臨
萬古光景常新而不可以一日無者也其間所
載遠而天理之精微近而人道之顯著幽而鬼
神明而禮樂廣大悉備誠未可以一二究其涯
涘姑以其大者言之故法象莫大於天地而有
陰陽剛柔之妙盖立天之道曰陰與陽立地之
punctuated:
第二問
梁建中
同考試官訓導周批：隨問隨荅，畧無疑碍，非老於性理者不能。歆羡，歆羡！
同考試官訓導華批：援據經傳，條荅詳明，盖嘗潜心於理學者。
考試官教諭陳批：據理條荅，畧無所遺。
考試官教諭張批：敷對無遺，必博學之士也。

文以載道，而《六經》、《四書》則萬世之至文也；學以明道，而《六經》、《四書》則萬世之正學也。學者因文以窮理，窮理以明道，則聖賢所載之微辭奥義，一以貫之而無疑矣。請承明問而畧評之。夫《六經》、《四書》之行于世，猶日月星辰之麗乎天，照臨萬古，光景常新，而不可以一日無者也。其間所載，遠而天理之精微，近而人道之顯著，幽而鬼神，明而禮樂，廣大悉備，誠未可以一二究其涯涘。姑以其大者言之：故法象莫大於天地，而有陰陽剛柔之妙。盖立天之道，曰陰與陽；立地之…
translation_en:
Second Question
Liang Jianzhong 梁建中
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Zhou 周 comments: "Answering each question in turn without the slightest hesitation or hindrance—no one who is not deeply seasoned in the philosophy of human nature and principle (xingli 性理) could achieve this. Admirable, truly admirable!"
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Hua 華 comments: "Drawing upon the Classics and commentaries, he answers point by point with clarity and detail; surely he is one who has immersed his mind in the learning of Principle (lixue 理學)."
Examiner and Instructor Chen 陳 comments: "Grounded in principle, he replies point by point, leaving nothing out."
Examiner and Instructor Zhang 張 comments: "An exhaustive response omitting nothing; he must be a scholar of broad learning."

Literature is the vehicle for the Way, and the Six Classics and Four Books are the supreme literature for ten thousand generations; learning is that which illuminates the Way, and the Six Classics and Four Books are the orthodox learning for ten thousand generations. If scholars rely on the texts to exhaustively investigate principle, and exhaustively investigate principle in order to illuminate the Way, then the subtle words and profound meanings recorded by the sages and worthies can bethreaded together by a single unifying principle without any doubt. Allow me to take up your illustrious question and briefly discuss it. Now, the circulation of the Six Classics and Four Books in the world is like the sun, moon, and stars arrayed across the heavens, shining down upon ten thousand ages, their radiance ever new, such that the world cannot go a single day without them. What is recorded therein—from the distant, subtle essence of Heavenly Principle, to the near, manifest reality of the human Way; from ghosts and spirits in the unseen realm, to rites and music in the visible world—is vast and all-encompassing, such that one truly cannot exhaust its boundless limits by citing just a point or two. Let me tentatively speak of its main outlines: No model or phenomenon is greater than Heaven and Earth, and within them lies the wondrous operation of yin and yang, firmness and gentleness. For that which establishes the Way of Heaven is called yin and yang; that which establishes the Way of Earth…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
道曰柔與剛一陰一陽而四時行焉一剛一柔
而四維定焉非天地之至妙者歟陰陽莫妙於
鬼神而不無大小費隱之别如晅之以日月潤
之以風雨是其大也而郊則天神格廟則人鬼
饗非小歟視弗見聽弗聞是其隱也而體物如
在非費歟惟皇上帝降衷于民所謂命也而其
吉凶禍福亦皆天之所命然惟莫之致而至者
乃為正命彼桎梏者豈正命耶成之者性各一
太極所謂性也而彼聲色臭味亦皆人之所有
===
然道則責成於已養則付命於天君子豈謂性
耶天命之性率循於已非道乎而所謂道一者
盖言古今聖愚本同一性初無二理也道二者
盖言能法堯舜則為仁不法堯舜則不仁也而
五達道則自君臣以至朋友之交是焉率性之
道實得於已非德乎而所謂三德者則孝德敏
德至德是也六德則智仁聖義中和是也而九
德則自寛而栗以至強而毅是焉立人之道曰
仁與義是人道莫大於仁義矣然分而言之則
punctuated: 道曰柔與剛，一陰一陽而四時行焉，一剛一柔而四維定焉，非天地之至妙者歟？陰陽莫妙於鬼神，而不無大小費隱之别。如晅之以日月，潤之以風雨，是其大也；而郊則天神格，廟則人鬼饗，非小歟？視弗見、聽弗聞，是其隱也；而體物如在，非費歟？惟皇上帝，降衷于民，所謂命也；而其吉凶禍福，亦皆天之所命。然惟莫之致而至者乃為正命，彼桎梏者豈正命耶？成之者性，各一太極，所謂性也；而彼聲色臭味，亦皆人之所有。然道則責成於已，養則付命於天，君子豈謂性耶？天命之性，率循於已，非道乎？而所謂道一者，盖言古今聖愚本同一性，初無二理也；道二者，盖言能法堯、舜則為仁，不法堯、舜則不仁也；而五達道，則自君臣以至朋友之交是焉。率性之道，實得於已，非德乎？而所謂三德者，則孝德、敏德、至德是也；六德，則智、仁、聖、義、中、和是也；而九德，則自寛而栗以至強而毅是焉。立人之道曰仁與義，是人道莫大於仁義矣。然分而言之，則
translation_en: … Way of establishing earth is called softness and firmness. With alternating yin and yang, the four seasons proceed therein; with alternating firmness and softness, the four cardinal dimensions are fixed therein—is this not the ultimate subtlety of heaven and earth? In yin and yang, nothing is more subtle than ghosts and spirits (guishen), yet they are not without distinctions of great and small, of the manifest (fei) and the hidden (yin). For instance, warming things with the sun and moon and moistening them with wind and rain—this is their greatness; whereas at the suburban sacrifice the heavenly spirits arrive, and in the ancestral temple the human ghosts enjoy the offerings—is this not their smallness? Looking for them yet not seeing, listening for them yet not hearing—this is their hiddenness; whereas embodying things as if present everywhere—is this not their manifestness? The August Supreme Emperor bestows a moral sense upon the people: this is what is called the Mandate (ming). And good fortune and bad, calamity and blessing are likewise all ordained by Heaven. Yet only that which arrives without being brought on by oneself constitutes the proper Mandate; how could dying in fetters and handcuffs be the proper Mandate? That which completes it is human nature (xing), each possessing its own Supreme Ultimate (taiji): this is what is called nature. And those sounds, colors, odors, and flavors are likewise all things possessed by human beings. Yet as for the Way, its fulfillment is demanded of oneself, while as for sensory nourishment, it is left to the Mandate of Heaven—how could the noble person call those "nature"? When the nature conferred by Heaven's Mandate is followed in oneself, is that not the Way (dao)? What is called "the Way is one" means that ancient and modern, sage and fool originally share the same nature, there being from the beginning no twofold principle. That "there are two Ways" means that if one can model oneself on Yao and Shun, one is humane (ren), and if one does not model oneself on Yao and Shun, one is inhumane. And as for the five universal Ways, they extend from the relation between ruler and minister down to the intercourse of friends. When the Way of following one's nature is genuinely attained within oneself, is that not Virtue (de)? What are called the three virtues are filial virtue, earnest virtue, and supreme virtue; the six virtues are wisdom, humanity, sageness, righteousness, centrality, and harmony; and the nine virtues extend from "affable yet栗 [firm]" down to "strong yet resolute." To establish the Way of humanity is called humanity (ren) and righteousness (yi); thus in the Way of humanity nothing is greater than humanity and righteousness. Yet if we speak of them separately, then…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
仁為陽為健義為陰為順錯而言之則義主於
斷而亦未嘗不健仁主於愛而亦未嘗不順也
大禮與天地同節大樂與天地同和是制作莫
大於禮樂矣然以言其本則和敬是已以言其
末則玉帛鐘鼓是已故敬而將之以玉帛和而
發之以鐘鼓則本物備具情文並行可謂全矣
苟玉帛交錯而敬或不足鐘鼓鏗鏘而和或不
及不已偏耶誠乃真實無妄之謂天理之本然
也學者未能真實無妄而欲其真實無妄非人
===
道之當然乎忠恕盡己推己之謂此學者之事
動以人爾而夫子之道一以貫之非動以天者
乎至若后非賢不乂賢非后不食是君臣誠人
道之大倫也而道德功力則皇帝王伯之辨以
無為為德而其道上達知足以帥人者則公卿
大夫之辨焉要其所各當盡之道則孔子所以
告定公者至矣父兮生我母兮鞠我是父子誠
天屬之至親也而正服義服則嫡繼慈養之別
而繼別繼禰則大宗小宗之別焉論其所各當
punctuated: 仁為陽、為健，義為陰、為順；錯而言之，則義主於斷而亦未嘗不健，仁主於愛而亦未嘗不順也。大禮與天地同節，大樂與天地同和，是制作莫大於禮樂矣。然以言其本，則和、敬是已；以言其末，則玉帛、鐘鼓是已。故敬而將之以玉帛，和而發之以鐘鼓，則本物備具，情文並行，可謂全矣。苟玉帛交錯而敬或不足，鐘鼓鏗鏘而和或不及，不已偏耶？誠乃真實無妄之謂，天理之本然也。學者未能真實無妄，而欲其真實無妄，非人道之當然乎？忠恕，盡己、推己之謂，此學者之事，動以人爾；而夫子之道一以貫之，非動以天者乎？至若后非賢不乂，賢非后不食，是君臣誠人道之大倫也。而道德功力，則皇、帝、王、伯之辨；以無為為德，而其道上達，知足以帥人者，則公、卿、大夫之辨焉。要其所各當盡之道，則孔子所以告定公者至矣。父兮生我，母兮鞠我，是父子誠天屬之至親也。而正服、義服，則嫡、繼、慈、養之別；而繼別、繼禰，則大宗、小宗之別焉。論其所各當
translation_en: …benevolence (ren) corresponds to yang and vigor, whereas righteousness (yi) corresponds to yin and compliance; yet if we speak of them in their interplay, righteousness is centered on decisiveness and thus is never without vigor, while benevolence is centered on love and thus is never without compliance. "Great ritual shares the same regulation as Heaven and Earth; great music shares the same harmony as Heaven and Earth"—thus among human institutions none is greater than ritual and music. Yet if we speak of their root, it is simply harmony and reverence; if we speak of their branches, it is simply jade and silk, bells and drums. Therefore, when reverence is conveyed through jade and silk, and harmony is expressed through bells and drums, both root and outward things are complete, and inner feeling and outward form proceed together; this may be called perfection. If, however, jade and silk are exchanged in profusion while reverence is perhaps lacking, or bells and drums resound clangorously while harmony falls short, is that not already one-sided? Sincerity (cheng) means being true, real, and free from falsity—the inherent state of Heavenly Principle. For a student who is not yet able to be true, real, and free from falsity to desire to become so—is this not the proper duty of the human way? Conscientiousness and altruism (zhongshu) mean doing one's utmost and extending oneself to others; this is the business of the learner, acting through what is human. Yet the Way of the Master [Confucius] binds it all together with a single thread—is that not acting through Heaven? As for the saying, "The sovereign without the worthy cannot govern, and the worthy without the sovereign cannot be fed," this shows that ruler and minister are truly a great relationship of the human way. Moral virtue and forceful achievement mark the distinction among the August Ones (huang), the Emperors (di), the Kings (wang), and the Hegemons (ba); taking non-action as virtue, having one's way reach upward, and possessing wisdom sufficient to lead others mark the distinctions among dukes (gong), ministers (qing), and grand masters (dafu). In summing up the way that each ought to fulfill, what Confucius told Duke Ding (Dinggong) is the ultimate statement. "O father, who begot me! O mother, who nourished me!"—this shows that father and son are truly the closest of Heaven-ordained kin. Canonical mourning grades (zhengfu) and principle-based mourning grades (yifu) mark the distinctions among the legal wife (di), stepmother (ji), foster mother (ci), and adoptive mother (yang); succeeding the founder of a separate lineage (jiebieli) and succeeding the father's shrine (jini) mark the distinction between the great lineage (dazong) and the lesser lineage (xiaozong). If we discuss the mourning that each ought…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
為之服則諸儒所以載於禮記者詳矣凡若此
者信皆天理人道之大端而凡學者所當講也
第愚生天與凡近問學功疎而於道猶望洋惟
不鄙夷而進教焉則幸甚
第三問
林會
同考試官教諭鄭批博以備衆言公以折羣議此子
其殆學術正識見高而毀譽
不足以動其心者歟
===
考試官教諭陳批備紛紛之議論而以義利邪
正折其衷其博而能約之士也
考試官教諭張批不規規於問目而議論淵如
文彩燁如是必陋樂毅而志
孔明者
甚矣古人之難盡知也亦甚矣載籍之難盡信
也盖載籍浩浩論議紛紛或舉其一而遺其二
或具其事而畧其心卒至是非失真而古人之
賢否邪正莫之辨矣必考其時跡其事究其心
punctuated:
為之服，則諸儒所以載於《禮記》者詳矣。凡若此者，信皆天理人道之大端，而凡學者所當講也。第愚生天與凡近，問學功疎，而於道猶望洋。惟不鄙夷而進教焉，則幸甚。
第三問
林會 〔同考試官教諭鄭批：博以備衆言，公以折羣議。此子其殆學術正、識見高，而毀譽不足以動其心者歟？考試官教諭陳批：備紛紛之議論，而以義利邪正折其衷，其博而能約之士也。考試官教諭張批：不規規於問目，而議論淵如，文彩燁如，是必陋樂毅而志孔明者。〕
甚矣，古人之難盡知也！亦甚矣，載籍之難盡信也！盖載籍浩浩，論議紛紛，或舉其一而遺其二，或具其事而畧其心，卒至是非失真，而古人之賢否邪正莫之辨矣。必考其時、跡其事、究其心，
translation_en:
… mourning garments one ought to wear for them, what the various scholars have recorded in the Record of Rites (Liji) is detailed indeed. All such matters as these are truly the great fundamentals of Heavenly principle and the human Way, which all scholars ought to study and discuss. Yet I, an ignorant student, was endowed by Heaven with ordinary and shallow capacities; my efforts in learning and inquiry have been negligent, and toward the Way I still gaze out as if bewildered at the vast ocean. If only you do not disdain me as rustic and instead summon me forward to instruct me, I shall be most fortunate.

Third Question
Lin Hui 林會 [Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Zheng 鄭: Broad in marshaling the words of the many, and impartial in arbitrating the debates of the crowd. Is this young man not one whose scholarship is orthodox, whose insight is lofty, and whose mind neither slander nor praise is sufficient to sway? Comment by Examiner and Instructor Chen 陳: He sets forth the tangled profusion of arguments and arbitrates among them by the standards of righteousness versus profit, crookedness versus rectitude; he is a scholar of broad learning who is yet able to bring it back to essentials. Comment by Examiner and Instructor Zhang 張: Not narrowly bound by the points of the question, his arguments are deep as an abyss and his literary brilliance shines forth; he must surely be one who looks down upon Yue Yi 樂毅 and sets his ambition upon Kongming 孔明 (Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮).]

Extreme indeed is the difficulty of fully knowing the ancients! And extreme indeed is the difficulty of fully trusting written records! For written records are vast and boundless, and their discussions and judgments are manifold and confused: some cite one aspect while omitting two others; some recount the deeds in full while passing over the intentions behind them. In the end, right and wrong lose their truth, and one can no longer distinguish the worthy from the unworthy, or the crooked from the upright, among the ancients. One must examine their times, trace their deeds, and probe their hearts, …

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
然後庶幾焉使不出此則雖同時而仕同堂而
語十人而書一人之事亦各不同蓋聞見有詳
畧文辭有工拙意向有高下坐此數者已多失
真矣況於數百載之下或千餘年之後耳不聞
其言也目不睹其事也意揣心搆以補其所不
足而增其所未備則所以失其真者不尤多乎
哉是故觀載籍與儒先君子之論在執事猶衆
難填胸羣疑滿腹況於迂愚之左見乎請因明
問所及而陳之燕之樂毅下齊七十餘城而即
===
墨與莒不拔夏侯太初謂其庶幾湯武蘇子瞻
謂王道不可以小用小用之則亡而以其為行
王道之過且湯武所以伐人之國者曷嘗有利
天下之心哉不忍斯民之塗炭挾大義而拯救
之是以東征西怨南征北怨皆曰奚為後我使
取一毫之非義殺一介之不辜雖奉海内之籍
而歸之湯武不肯正目而視也王道蕩蕩大用
之則大治小用之則小治猶之菽粟少食之則
不死恒食之則充實奚可以菽粟不可少食而
punctuated:
然後庶幾焉。使不出此，則雖同時而仕、同堂而語，十人而書一人之事，亦各不同。蓋聞見有詳畧，文辭有工拙，意向有高下，坐此數者，已多失真矣；況於數百載之下，或千餘年之後，耳不聞其言也，目不睹其事也，意揣心搆，以補其所不足而增其所未備，則所以失其真者不尤多乎哉！是故觀載籍與儒先君子之論，在執事猶衆難填胸、羣疑滿腹，況於迂愚之左見乎？請因明問所及而陳之。

燕之樂毅下齊七十餘城，而即墨與莒不拔。夏侯太初謂其庶幾湯、武，蘇子瞻謂「王道不可以小用，小用之則亡」，而以其為行王道之過。且湯、武所以伐人之國者，曷嘗有利天下之心哉？不忍斯民之塗炭，挾大義而拯救之，是以東征西怨，南征北怨，皆曰「奚為後我」。使取一毫之非義，殺一介之不辜，雖奉海内之籍而歸之，湯、武不肯正目而視也。王道蕩蕩，大用之則大治，小用之則小治。猶之菽粟，少食之則不死，恒食之則充實，奚可以菽粟不可少食，而
translation_en:
…only then may one come close to the truth. If one does not proceed in this manner, then even among those who served at the same time and conversed in the same hall, if ten people were to record the deeds of a single person, each account would differ. This is because what is heard and seen varies in detail, literary expression varies in skill, and intentions vary in loftiness. On account of these several factors, much of the truth is already lost. How much more so several hundred or over a thousand years later, when one's ears have not heard their words and one's eyes have not witnessed their deeds! When people rely on conjecture and mental fabrication to supply what is lacking and add to what is incomplete, is not the loss of truth even greater? Therefore, when examining written records and the discussions of former Confucian gentlemen, even Your Excellency finds your breast filled with numerous difficulties and your mind brimming with doubts—how much more so for the biased views of someone as迂腐 [pedantic] and foolish as I! Allow me to set forth my thoughts by following the points raised in your enlightened question.

Yue Yi 樂毅 of Yan 燕 captured more than seventy cities of Qi 齊, yet Jimo 即墨 and Ju 莒 remained untaken. Xiahou Taichu 夏侯太初 (Xiahou Xuan 夏侯玄) claimed that he nearly matched Tang 湯 and Wu 武, whereas Su Zizhan 蘇子瞻 (Su Shi 蘇軾) argued that "the Kingly Way cannot be applied on a small scale; to apply it on a small scale leads to ruin," faulting him for the error of practicing the Kingly Way. Yet when Tang and Wu attacked the states of others, how could they ever have harbored a desire to profit from the world? Unable to bear the people's mire and charcoal of suffering, they upheld great righteousness to rescue them. Thus, when they campaigned in the east, the west complained, and when they campaigned in the south, the north complained, all saying, "Why does he leave us until last?" Had it required taking a single hair's breadth unrighteously or killing a single innocent person, even if the registers of the entire realm had been presented in submission to them, Tang and Wu would not have deigned to look directly at them. The Kingly Way is broad and level: applied on a grand scale, it brings grand order; applied on a small scale, it brings small order. It is like beans and grain: eating a little keeps one from dying, while eating them regularly makes one full and strong. How could one say that because beans and grain should not be eaten in small amounts, one would…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
寧噉糠籺哉彼樂毅生當戰國之時為魏使燕
因燕昭王好賢遂委質為臣未幾至上將軍時
齊最收怨於諸侯而燕昭怨之特甚故毅得以
承令而約趙楚韓魏與燕之兵併護之以伐齊
下齊之國都不㧞施仁敷惠以慰其父兄子弟
乃遷其重器寶貨於燕齊民固已怨入骨髓矣
毅之師特報讐圖利之舉耳幸而下七十餘城
畏其兵威力屈而服之非心服也及兵威既振
所不下者即墨與莒毅之心以為在吾腹中一
===
指顧而取之有餘矣其心肆氣怠士剉而二城
之怨方堅齊民之心方奮用堅奮之人而禦怠
肆已剉之讐雖百萬之師固不㧞拔二城之人
非可拔而姑存之使自服也亦非愛其民而不
以兵屠之也湯武以一國征諸國而人靡有不
服者毅以諸國征二小邑且猶叛之湯武以義
而毅以利王道以正而霸以譎事之所以不同
也遠矣不知夏侯太初何自而謂其庶幾湯武
蘇子瞻何自而謂其行王道之過也漢之孔明
punctuated: 寧噉糠籺哉？彼樂毅生當戰國之時，為魏使燕，因燕昭王好賢，遂委質為臣，未幾至上將軍。時齊最收怨於諸侯，而燕昭怨之特甚，故毅得以承令，而約趙、楚、韓、魏與燕之兵，併護之以伐齊。下齊之國都，不㧞施仁敷惠，以慰其父兄子弟，乃遷其重器寶貨於燕，齊民固已怨入骨髓矣。毅之師，特報讐圖利之舉耳。幸而下七十餘城，畏其兵威，力屈而服之，非心服也。及兵威既振，所不下者即墨與莒，毅之心以為在吾腹中，一指顧而取之有餘矣。其心肆氣怠士剉，而二城之怨方堅，齊民之心方奮。用堅奮之人，而禦怠肆已剉之讐，雖百萬之師，固不㧞拔二城之人。非可拔而姑存之使自服也，亦非愛其民而不以兵屠之也。湯、武以一國征諸國，而人靡有不服者；毅以諸國征二小邑，且猶叛之。湯、武以義，而毅以利；王道以正，而霸以譎，事之所以不同也遠矣。不知夏侯太初何自而謂其庶幾湯、武，蘇子瞻何自而謂其行王道之過也？漢之孔明，
translation_en: …prefer to eat chaff and husks instead? Now, Yue Yi 樂毅 lived during the Warring States period. Serving as an envoy from Wei 魏 to Yan 燕, because King Zhao of Yan 燕昭王 loved worthy men, he presented a pledge and became his subject, before long rising to Upper General (shang jiangjun). At that time, Qi 齊 had incurred the greatest resentment among the feudal lords, and King Zhao of Yan resented it most bitterly. Thus, Yi was able to receive orders to form an alliance with the troops of Zhao 趙, Chu 楚, Han 韓, and Wei 魏 together with those of Yan, commanding their combined forces to attack Qi. When he captured the capital of Qi, he could not [?] bestow benevolence and spread favor to comfort its elders and youths, but instead removed its prized vessels and precious goods to Yan; the people of Qi already felt resentment penetrating to the marrow of their bones. Yi's campaign was merely an act of avenging a feud and seeking profit. Although he was fortunate enough to capture more than seventy cities, they submitted because they feared his military might and their strength was exhausted, not because they submitted in their hearts. Once his military might had been displayed and the only places not yet captured were Jimo 即墨 and Ju 莒, Yi thought in his heart that they were already in his belly, and that he could more than easily take them at the point of a finger or the turn of a glance. His mind grew lax, his spirit slackened, and his soldiers were blunted, whereas the resentment of the two cities was just then firm and the hearts of the people of Qi were just then roused. Using resolute and roused men to resist a lax, slackened, and already blunted enemy, even with an army of a million, he certainly could not [?] uproot the people of the two cities. It was not that they could have been taken and he provisionally spared them so they would submit of their own accord; nor was it that he loved their people and therefore refrained from slaughtering them with troops. Tang 湯 and Wu 武 used a single state to punish multiple states, and there were none who did not submit; Yi used multiple states to attack two small towns, and yet they still rebelled against him. Tang and Wu acted out of righteousness, whereas Yi acted out of profit; the Kingly Way operates through rectitude, whereas the Hegemon's Way operates through deceit—the reasons why their affairs differed are vast indeed! One does not know on what basis Xiahou Taichu 夏侯太初 (Xiahou Xuan 夏侯玄) said that he came close to Tang and Wu, or on what basis Su Zizhan 蘇子瞻 (Su Shi 蘇軾) said that his fault lay in practicing the Kingly Way! As for Kongming 孔明 (Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮) of the Han 漢…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
志在恢復炎祚而大業未就以卒陳壽謂其亞
匹管蕭又謂其連歲動衆未能成功盖應變將
畧非其所長且管仲相桓公覇諸侯一匡天下
民到于今稱之功亦偉矣而乃不能正身脩德
以致主于王道蕭何輔高祖成帝業發蹤指示
而匡輔之功居多養民致賢而勸君之意尤切
烈亦盛矣而亦不能積誠法古以聿興夫禮樂
若吾孔明生當三國寄跡隆中漢之昭烈三顧
草廬幡然而起未幾身都將相是時吳為最強
===
魏次之而漢獨以區區之蜀間於二雄而欲信
大義於天下以復漢祖之炎祚其時其事尤為
難也然以布衣至於為相而人不以為速以討
賊為己任而不任將帥人不以為自用斷一國
之政賞罰予奪一無所貸人不以為專彼二國
之司馬懿周魯張陸之徒皆不能及顧乃深有
資於僚佐而懇懇求忠藎之言以孔明之賢豈
待乎僚佐之益舉全蜀之士豈復有出於孔明
智慮之右乎賢人君子之用心也遠而期望也
punctuated: 志在恢復炎祚，而大業未就以卒。陳壽謂其亞匹管、蕭，又謂其「連歲動衆，未能成功，盖應變將畧，非其所長」。且管仲相桓公，覇諸侯，一匡天下，民到于今稱之，功亦偉矣，而乃不能正身脩德，以致主于王道；蕭何輔高祖，成帝業，發蹤指示，而匡輔之功居多，養民致賢，而勸君之意尤切，烈亦盛矣，而亦不能積誠法古，以聿興夫禮樂。若吾孔明，生當三國，寄跡隆中，漢之昭烈三顧草廬，幡然而起，未幾身都將相。是時吳為最強，魏次之，而漢獨以區區之蜀間於二雄，而欲信大義於天下，以復漢祖之炎祚，其時其事，尤為難也。然以布衣至於為相，而人不以為速；以討賊為己任，而不任將帥，人不以為自用；斷一國之政，賞罰予奪，一無所貸，人不以為專。彼二國之司馬懿、周、魯、張、陸之徒皆不能及，顧乃深有資於僚佐，而懇懇求忠藎之言。以孔明之賢，豈待乎僚佐之益？舉全蜀之士，豈復有出於孔明智慮之右乎？賢人君子之用心也遠，而期望也…
translation_en: …his ambition was set on restoring the fiery mandate of the Han, yet he died before the great enterprise was accomplished. Chen Shou 陳壽 said that he was a close match to Guan Zhong 管仲 and Xiao He 蕭何, and also remarked that "year after year he mobilized the masses without achieving success, probably because flexible military strategy was not his strong suit." Now, Guan Zhong assisted Duke Huan 桓公, established hegemony over the feudal lords, and brought order to the entire realm, so that the people praise him down to the present day—his achievements were indeed伟大. Yet he was unable to rectify himself and cultivate virtue so as to lead his ruler onto the Kingly Way. Xiao He assisted Emperor Gaozu 高祖 in accomplishing the imperial enterprise; in pointing out the quarry and giving direction, his merits of assistance and support were the greatest, and in nourishing the people and attracting the worthy, his earnestness in exhorting his ruler was especially keen—his exploits were indeed splendid. Yet he too was unable to accumulate sincerity and model himself on antiquity so as to bring about the flourishing of ritual and music. As for our Kongming 孔明 [Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮], he was born in the era of the Three Kingdoms and lived in seclusion at Longzhong 隆中. When Zhaolie 昭烈 [Liu Bei 劉備] of Han paid three visits to his thatched cottage, he rose up with a change of heart, and before long held in his own person the offices of both general and chief minister. At that time, Wu 吳 was the strongest,[?] with Wei 魏 second to it, while Han alone, with the tiny territory of Shu 蜀 wedged between the two great powers, sought to extend great righteousness throughout the realm and restore the fiery mandate of the Han founder—both the timing and the undertaking were especially difficult. Even so, he rose from a commoner to become chief minister, and people did not consider his promotion too rapid; he took the chastisement of the rebels as his personal responsibility rather than delegating it to other generals, and people did not consider him self-willed; he decided the governance of the entire state, dispensing rewards and punishments, granting and taking away without the slightest leniency, and people did not consider him autocratic. None of those in the other two states—men the likes of Sima Yi 司馬懿, Zhou Yu 周瑜, Lu Su 魯肅, Zhang Zhao 張昭, and Lu Xun 陸遜—could equal him. Even so, he relied deeply upon his subordinates and associates, earnestly seeking words of loyal devotion. Given Kongming's worthiness, how could he really have needed the help of his subordinates? And among all the scholars of Shu, how could there have been anyone who surpassed Kongming in wisdom and foresight? The minds of worthy men and noble men reach far, and their aspirations are…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
大常自見其不足而不見其有餘惟不自用其
才知也故能擧用天下之才智苟露其才智與
人角錙銖分寸以求勝則凡有才智者皆吾敵
也吾安得而用之哉至於出師一表無愧乎伊
訓說命之言八陣一圖彷佛乎黃帝太公之制
魏之司馬懿用兵如神筭無遺策每與孔明交
鋒動輒敗北是以其徒有畏之如虎之譏時孔
明孤軍遠出粮餉不繼懿以銳師大衆乘氣而
扞禦之猶狼狽如許至受巾幗婦人之服而不
===
敢出氣孔明既卒而懿追之姜維令楊儀反旗
鳴鼓若向懿者懿遂斂軍以退百姓為之諺曰
死諸葛猶走生仲達及懿行孔明營壘處所嘆
曰天下竒才也况五丈原之屯恩信行於中原
威畧震乎遠邇屯田積聚軍旅散於民居而皆
相安三代之兵若時雨孔明者庶幾矣故論諸
葛之出處可比伊尹正大之出處也諸葛之人
才可亞伊周王佐之大才也而其心則一於興
漢豈有一毫譎詐圖利之意哉特時事之難及
punctuated: 大，常自見其不足而不見其有餘。惟不自用其才知也，故能擧用天下之才智。苟露其才智，與人角錙銖分寸以求勝，則凡有才智者皆吾敵也，吾安得而用之哉？至於《出師》一表，無愧乎《伊訓》、《說命》之言；《八陣》一圖，彷佛乎黃帝、太公之制。魏之司馬懿用兵如神，筭無遺策，每與孔明交鋒，動輒敗北，是以其徒有「畏之如虎」之譏。時孔明孤軍遠出，粮餉不繼，懿以銳師大衆乘氣而扞禦之，猶狼狽如許，至受巾幗婦人之服而不敢出氣。孔明既卒而懿追之，姜維令楊儀反旗鳴鼓，若向懿者，懿遂斂軍以退。百姓為之諺曰：「死諸葛猶走生仲達。」及懿行孔明營壘處所，嘆曰：「天下竒才也！」况五丈原之屯，恩信行於中原，威畧震乎遠邇；屯田積聚，軍旅散於民居而皆相安。三代之兵若時雨，孔明者庶幾矣。故論諸葛之出處，可比伊尹正大之出處也；諸葛之人才，可亞伊、周王佐之大才也。而其心則一於興漢，豈有一毫譎詐圖利之意哉？特時事之難，及
translation_en:
… grand, always seeing their own inadequacies rather than their surpluses. Only because he did not rely solely on his own talent and wisdom was he able to employ the talent and wisdom of the entire world. If one flaunts one's talent and wisdom, competing with others over every tiny fraction just to seek victory, then all who possess talent and wisdom become one's enemies—how then could one make use of them?

As for his single Memorial on Deploying the Troops (Chushi biao), it is entirely worthy of the words of the Instructions of Yi (Yi xun) and the Charge to Yue (Yue ming); his single Diagram of the Eight Formations (Bazhen tu) closely resembles the systems of the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi) and the Grand Duke (Taigong). Sima Yi 司馬懿 of Wei deployed troops like a god and planned without a single oversight, yet whenever he crossed swords with Kong明 [Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮], he was routinely defeated, which led to the taunt among his own peers that he "feared him like a tiger." At the time, Kongming led an isolated army on a distant expedition with unreliable grain supplies, whereas Yi defended against him with elite troops and a massive host riding on high morale. Even so, Yi was reduced to such dire straits that he accepted the gift of a woman's headdress and garments without daring to utter a breath of protest. After Kongming died and Yi pursued him, Jiang Wei 姜維 ordered Yang Yi 楊儀 to turn the banners around and beat the drums as if advancing toward Yi, whereupon Yi promptly pulled back his troops and retreated. The common people made a proverb about this, saying: "A dead Zhuge still puts a living Zhongda [Sima Yi] to flight." When Yi inspected the site of Kongming's camps and ramparts, he sighed and said: "He was truly a wondrous talent of the world!"

Moreover, during his encampment at the Wuzhang Plains (Wuzhangyuan), his benevolence and trustworthiness spread throughout the Central Plains, and his martial prestige and strategy shook lands far and near. While establishing military agricultural colonies and stockpiling supplies, his troops were quartered among civilian dwellings, yet all lived in mutual peace. The armies of the Three Dynasties were like timely rain—Kongming came very close to this ideal! Therefore, if we judge Zhuge's decision to emerge into public service or remain in retirement, it can be compared to the upright and noble course of Yi Yin 伊尹; as for Zhuge's personal talent, he ranks second only to the great kingly-assistant talents of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou (Zhougong 周公). And his heart was wholly devoted to restoring the Han—how could there have been the slightest trace of deceit or self-seeking profit in his intentions? It was only because of the difficulties of the times and affairs, and when…

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
不幸五十四歲而卒天不祚漢可勝嘆哉使其
不死則漢室可興禮樂有望矣彼陳壽之徒以
形跡成敗論人而比之為管蕭又謂應變將畧
非其所長所言之繆不攻而自破矣若論其極
則樂毅非管蕭之匹而孔明直亞伊周豈戰國
秦漢之士可及哉噫太初曲士不足論獨惜陳
壽蘇子之易其言耳此後世之論失其真者然
也若夫孔明養高隆中之日嘗自比管仲樂毅
而時人已莫之許盖孔明特主於撥亂繼絶一
===
時自寓之言耳豈不知二人而甘附之哉然惟
豪傑然後能知豪傑當時盖少孔明之俦故雖
自比管樂而人亦莫之許無足恠焉此又當時
之論失其真者然也雖然論人失真非獨古昔
也幸執事裁而表章之以示警策云謹對
第四問
林廷璋
同考試官訓導周批〔士風一策正欲觀學者趨向何如此答詳於事實末復歸重於〕
punctuated:
不幸五十四歲而卒。天不祚漢，可勝嘆哉！使其不死，則漢室可興，禮樂有望矣。彼陳壽之徒，以形跡成敗論人，而比之為管、蕭，又謂「應變將畧，非其所長」，所言之繆，不攻而自破矣。若論其極，則樂毅非管、蕭之匹，而孔明直亞伊、周，豈戰國、秦、漢之士可及哉！噫，太初曲士，不足論，獨惜陳壽、蘇子之易其言耳。此後世之論失其真者然也。若夫孔明養高隆中之日，嘗自比管仲、樂毅，而時人已莫之許。盖孔明特主於撥亂繼絶，一時自寓之言耳，豈不知二人而甘附之哉？然惟豪傑然後能知豪傑，當時盖少孔明之俦，故雖自比管、樂，而人亦莫之許，無足恠焉。此又當時之論失其真者然也。雖然，論人失真，非獨古昔也，幸執事裁而表章之，以示警策云。謹對。

第四問
林廷璋
同考試官訓導周批〔士風一策，正欲觀學者趨向何如。此答詳於事實，末復歸重於〕
translation_en:
… unfortunately died at the age of fifty-four. Heaven did not bless the Han; how can one lament it enough! Had he not died, the House of Han could have been restored, and there would have been hope for rites and music. People like Chen Shou 陳壽 judged men by outward traces of success and failure, comparing him to Guan Zhong 管仲 and Xiao He 蕭何, and further claiming that "adaptive military strategy was not his strong suit." The fallacy of such words collapses of itself without needing to be attacked. If we discuss the highest standard, Yue Yi 樂毅 was not the peer of Guan Zhong and Xiao He, while Kongming 孔明 (Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮) was directly second only to Yi Yin 伊尹 and the Duke of Zhou 周公—how could the scholars of the Warring States, Qin, and Han ever match him! Alas, a narrow-minded scholar like Taichu 太初 (Xiahou Xuan 夏侯玄) is not worth discussing; I only regret that Chen Shou and Master Su 蘇子 (Su Xun 蘇洵) spoke so lightly. Such is how the judgments of later generations lost the truth of the matter. As for the days when Kongming cultivated lofty seclusion in Longzhong 隆中, he once compared himself to Guan Zhong and Yue Yi, yet his contemporaries did not grant him even that. In truth, Kongming was simply focused on quelling chaos and restoring a severed line, so those were merely words of temporary self-expression; how could he not have understood those two men and willingly attached himself to them? Yet only a hero can truly know a hero. At that time there were few who were Kongming's peers, so even though he compared himself to Guan and Yue, people still did not acknowledge it—which is no wonder at all. Such, in turn, is how the judgments of his own time lost the truth of the matter. Even so, failing to grasp the truth in judging men is not unique to antiquity. I hope that Your Excellency will adjudicate and bring this to light, so as to serve as an admonition and spur. I respectfully reply.

Fourth Question
Lin Tingzhang 林廷璋
Comment by Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Zhou 周: 〔The policy question on literati customs was intended precisely to observe the orientation of the scholars. This answer is detailed in its historical facts, and at the end returns to place emphasis on…〕

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
誠則其為人可想矣一萬何永
考試官教諭陳批歷歴具實詳荅足見博覧

三代而上士風之議未聞三代而下士風之議

From the Three Dynasties and earlier, discussions of the ethos of literati were unheard of; from the Three Dynasties onward, discussions of the ethos of literati first became prominent. Now, the reason the ethos of literati was unheard of is that worldly customs were pure and generous, and everyone cherished virtue, so there was nothing calling for discussion; the reason the ethos of literati first became prominent is that worldly customs grew daily more frivolous, and people were no longer like those of antiquity, so there arose matters calling for discussion. Allow me to follow your enlightened question and briefly set this forth.

Now, when a scholar is born between heaven and earth, how could it merely be a matter of speaking like a Confucian and acting like a Confucian, wearing a Confucian cap and dressing in Confucian robes? What makes him truly so is simply valuing sincerity, quiet retirement, deferential yielding, and incorruptibility. Therefore, the ancients trained and nurtured customs to make literati know how to respect themselves, and esteemed reputation and integrity to cause literati to know where to set their minds. That is why they were so urgent about this and did not slacken.

In later times, as in the Song dynasty, when Emperor Taizong composed poems to warn against deceit and extravagance, and Emperor Zhenzong composed poems to denounce opportunistic competition, how could literati fail to be sincere and quietly retiring? When they dismissed the younger kinsmen of Li Fang 李昉 to punish usurpation, and enrolled the descendants of [Fan] Wensou 范溫叟 to admonish against venality, how could literati fail to be deferentially yielding and incorruptible? Therefore, at that time everyone strove to cultivate their conduct, greatly revitalizing the ethos of literati.

For instance, when Hu Su 胡宿 was Administrating the Judicial Control Office, there happened to be a Tax Overseer who fell short of his quota; someone tried to stop Hu from reporting it honestly, and His Excellency said, "I have served our sovereign until my hair is now white; I cannot bear to deceive my ruler by even a hair's breadth." 之除相曰臣以駑朽請薦相才之寇準焉杜祁

translation_en: … how could I dare deceive my sovereign?' As for one who, while serving in an Academician post (guanzhi), did not attend banquets and gatherings and frankly answered his sovereign that it was because of poverty—that was Yan Shu 晏殊. And one who, while serving as a Palace Official (gongguan), privately went into the market to drink and likewise frankly answered the Emperor that it was because of poverty—that was Lu Zongdao 魯宗道. When these gentlemen regulated their conduct in such a manner, was not the ethos of honesty and sincerity clearly manifest? Qian Ruoshui 錢若水, serving as Assistant Military Affairs Commissioner (Shumi fushi), requested to be relieved of his confidential duties because his mother was aged. Han Jiansu 韓見素 [Han Yuan 韓援], serving as Investigating Censor (Jiancha yushi), grew weary of the scramble for advancement and submitted a memorial asking to retire from office. As for one who was recommended as a metropolitan graduate (jinshi), yet declined to sit for the Palace Examination because his father was a Grand Councilor—that was Han Chiguo 韓持國 [Han Wei 韓維]. And one who ascended the Imperial Roster (huangjia) and, when his name was memorialized as first, refused to step forward and claim it for himself—that was Fan Jingren 范景仁 [Fan Zhen 范鎮]. When several gentlemen established their minds in this way, was not the ethos of calm modesty and self-effacement flourishing? As for Lord Zhang Yong 張詠, when examined in Daming 大名, he yielded first place to Zhang Tan 張覃 of the same commandery; Lord Cai Qi 蔡齊, when examined in Laizhou 萊州, deferred the top selection to his fellow villager Shi Fang 史方. Even to the point that when Bi Wenjian 畢文簡 [Bi Shi'an 畢士安] was appointed Grand Councilor, he said: 'As your servant is dull and worn out, I beg to recommend Kou Zhun 寇準, who has the talent of a Grand Councilor.' And when Duke Qi of Du 杜祁公 [Du Yan 杜衍] left his post as Grand Councilor, he said: 'Lacking talent as I do, I truly fear I have long obstructed the path of the worthy.' Such was the deference and yielding of these several gentlemen. When the Duke of Lai 萊公 [Kou Zhun] held the position of Grand Councilor, his home was cramped and narrow, with no ground on which to erect towers or terraces; when Zhao Bian 趙抃 governed Chengdu 成都, his heart abided in incorruptible purity, so that he even put away his pet tortoise and crane. Even to the point that when Yu Jing 余靖 served as Pacification Commissioner (Anfu shi) of Guangxi 廣西, upon his return he did not carry back a single item from the southern seas; and when Shen Lun 沈倫 served as Land and Water Transport Commissioner (Shuilu zhuanyun shi), upon his return he had only a few scrolls of books and charts. title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
言之則以誠實為本然非誠實則三者不可虛
行矣且司馬公之辭翰林王安石之辭舘職其
推遜一也議者以温公為是而荆公為非温公
之辭歸西洛荆公欲投老鍾山其恬退一也論
者以温公為得而荆公為失温公不事生產荆
公不自奉養均之為清亷也議者以温公為真
而荆公為詐何也重厚之士其處己以誠好名
之士其處己以不誠温公忠厚之士而荆公好
名之士也故有彼此習尚之殊又豈不關於誠
===
與不誠也哉此誠實者所以為三者之本也愚
也棲迹螢窓潜心蠹簡素思以名節存心嘗有
考於是矣茲承明問聊槩述是以對幸執事進
而教焉
第五問
王惟節
同考試官訓導郁批〔策有考據有斷制篇末數語又能窺主司之意於言外舉而措之必有大過人者當拭目以俟〕
punctuated:
言之，則以誠實為本。然非誠實，則三者不可虛行矣。且司馬公之辭翰林，王安石之辭舘職，其推遜一也，議者以温公為是而荆公為非；温公之辭歸西洛，荆公欲投老鍾山，其恬退一也，論者以温公為得而荆公為失；温公不事生產，荆公不自奉養，均之為清亷也，議者以温公為真而荆公為詐，何也？重厚之士，其處己以誠；好名之士，其處己以不誠。温公忠厚之士，而荆公好名之士也。故有彼此習尚之殊，又豈不關於誠與不誠也哉？此誠實者，所以為三者之本也。愚也棲迹螢窓，潜心蠹簡，素思以名節存心，嘗有考於是矣。茲承明問，聊槩述是以對，幸執事進而教焉。

第五問
王惟節
同考試官訓導郁批〔策有考據，有斷制，篇末數語，又能窺主司之意於言外，舉而措之，必有大過人者，當拭目以俟。〕
translation_en:
… speaking of them as a whole, sincerity and truthfulness are the foundation. Without sincerity and truthfulness, the other three cannot be practiced in vain. Moreover, Sima Guang's (Duke Sima 司馬公) declining the Hanlin Academy and Wang Anshi's 王安shi declining a Historiography Academy post were identical in their modesty and deference, yet critics considered the Duke of Wen (Sima Guang 温公) right and the Duke of Jing (Wang Anshi 荆公) wrong. The Duke of Wen's taking leave to return to western Luoyang and the Duke of Jing's wishing to retire in old age to Mount Zhong were identical in their calm withdrawal from office, yet commentators considered the Duke of Wen to have succeeded and the Duke of Jing to have failed. The Duke of Wen did not occupied himself with family livelihood, and the Duke of Jing did not indulge in personal comfort; both were equally incorruptible, yet critics considered the Duke of Wen genuine and the Duke of Jing deceitful. Why is this? A grave and generous scholar conducts himself with sincerity; a scholar fond of reputation conducts himself with insincerity. The Duke of Wen was a loyal and generous scholar, whereas the Duke of Jing was a scholar fond of reputation. Therefore, even where there are differences in their respective habits and inclinations, how could it not hinge upon sincerity versus insincerity? Thus, sincerity and truthfulness are the foundation of the other three. In my simplicity, I have dwelt by the firefly-lit window and immersed my mind in worm-eaten bamboo slips; I have long sought to keep integrity and honor in my heart, and have previously examined these matters. Now, having received your enlightened question, I provisionally set forth this general account in reply, hoping that Your Excellency will bring me forward and instruct me.

Fifth Question
Wang Weijie 王惟節

title: 成化四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
考試官敎諭陳批〔答述不遺有用之學〕
考試官敎諭張批〔隨問隨答必有學之士也〕
嘗謂人臣之進諫於君也貴有其道又貴有其
時何也有其道矣而時不至焉則諫或不行不
可也有其時矣而或道已失焉則諫或不切其
可乎哉然必有其道有其時而後諫可行也今
承執事發策而以諫諍爲問是盖責望以古者
執節秉義之士而不以尋常目之也其用心抑
何厚耶請因明問而條陳之甚矣諫諍之多端
===
也有直諫者有諷諫者如石介之犯顏逆鱗叩
頭流血其名曰直宜也而或疑其激如趙公槩
之和容愉色微辭婉容其名曰諷宜也而或譏
其佞直旣不可諷又不可君子於此將何爲哉
愚嘗聞朱晦庵有云伊川之諫其至誠惻怛防
微慮遠旣發乎愛君之誠其涵養善端培殖治
本又合乎告君之道皆可以爲後世法此進諫
之有其道也又嘗聞吕東萊有云諫之道有三
難焉曰遠曰疎曰驟遠則勢不接疎則情不通

考試官敎諭陳批〔答述不遺，有用之學。〕
考試官敎諭張批〔隨問隨答，必有學之士也。〕

嘗謂人臣之進諫於君也，貴有其道，又貴有其時。何也？有其道矣，而時不至焉，則諫或不行，不可也；有其時矣，而或道已失焉，則諫或不切，其可乎哉？然必有其道、有其時，而後諫可行也。今承執事發策，而以諫諍爲問，是盖責望以古者執節秉義之士，而不以尋常目之也，其用心抑何厚耶！請因明問而條陳之。甚矣，諫諍之多端也！有直諫者，有諷諫者。如石介之犯顏逆鱗，叩頭流血，其名曰「直」，宜也，而或疑其激；如趙公槩之和容愉色，微辭婉容，其名曰「諷」，宜也，而或譏其佞。直旣不可，諷又不可，君子於此將何爲哉？愚嘗聞朱晦庵有云：「伊川之諫，其至誠惻怛，防微慮遠，旣發乎愛君之誠；其涵養善端，培殖治本，又合乎告君之道，皆可以爲後世法。」此進諫之有其道也。又嘗聞吕東萊有云：「諫之道有三難焉：曰遠，曰疎，曰驟。遠則勢不接，疎則情不通，

I have always held that when a minister presents remonstrance to his ruler, what is valued is having the right way, and also having the right time. Why is this? If one has the right way, yet the time has not arrived, then the remonstrance may not be put into practice—this will not do. If one has the right time, yet the way has perhaps been lost, then the remonstrance may not be pertinent—how could that do? Thus, only when there is both the right way and the right time can remonstrance be put into practice. Now, having received Your Excellency’s policy question asking about remonstrance and admonition, this is surely because you hold us to the expectations of the men of antiquity who upheld integrity and grasped righteousness, and do not regard us as ordinary men. How generous indeed is your intention! Allow me to set forth my points item by item in response to your enlightened inquiry.

Great indeed are the many varieties of remonstrance! There are those who remonstrate directly, and those who remonstrate by indirect suasion. For instance, Shi Jie 石介 braved the ruler’s countenance and brushed against the dragon’s逆鱗 [inverted scales], knocking his head on the ground until it bled; to call this "direct" is fitting, yet some suspected him of being overly strident. Or take Lord Zhao Gai 趙槩, with his harmonious countenance and pleasant expression, using subtle words and gentle demeanor; to call this "indirect suasion" is fitting, yet some ridiculed him as flattering. If directness will not do, and indirect suasion will not do either, what then is a gentleman to do in this situation?

I have heard that Zhu Huian 朱晦庵 (Zhu Xi 朱熹) once said: "The remonstrance of Yichuan 伊川 (Cheng Yi 程頤), in its utmost sincerity and earnestness, guarding against the incipient and planning for the distant future, sprang from the sincerity of loving his ruler; and in its nurturing of the beginnings of goodness and cultivating the root of governance, it also accorded with the proper way of advising a ruler. All of this can serve as a model for later generations." This is what is meant by presenting remonstrance with the right way. I have also heard that Lü Donglai 吕東萊 (Lü Zuqian 呂祖謙) once said: "In the way of remonstrance there are three difficulties: namely, being distant, being estranged, and being abrupt. When distant, one's position does not connect; when estranged, feelings are not communicated; …"
